lesson.title: No Price on the Vote: The Twenty-Fourth Amendment
lesson.summary: Ratified in January 1964, the Twenty-Fourth Amendment banned poll taxes in federal elections, eliminating one of the key tools Southern states had used for decades to keep Black citizens from voting.
lesson.body:
The Fifteenth Amendment, ratified in 1870, declared that the right to vote could not be denied on account of race. Beginning in the late nineteenth century, Southern states nonetheless found indirect ways around that guarantee, including literacy tests, so called grandfather clauses, and poll taxes, small fees required in order to vote that fell disproportionately hard on poor Black citizens, and some poor white citizens as well, effectively pricing many of them out of the ballot box.

By the mid-twentieth century, a handful of Southern states still charged poll taxes in elections. Civil rights advocates and their allies in Congress pushed for a constitutional amendment banning the practice, at least in federal elections. Congress proposed the amendment in 1962, and it was ratified by the required number of states by January 23, 1964.

The amendment's language is brief: it prohibits states from denying or abridging the right to vote in federal elections because of a failure to pay a poll tax or any other tax. Because it applied specifically to federal elections, some states initially continued to require poll taxes in state and local elections. That loophole closed in 1966, when the Supreme Court ruled in Harper v. Virginia Board of Elections that poll taxes in any election violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, ending the practice nationwide.

The Twenty-Fourth Amendment worked alongside the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and, soon after, the Voting Rights Act of 1965, which banned literacy tests, as part of a broader legal effort to dismantle the barriers that had kept the promise of the Fifteenth Amendment from being fully realized for nearly a century.
